questions.title: PL-600 Solution Architect: what does the exam cover and what is its current status?
questions.quick: PL-600 is the Power Platform Solution Architect exam. When I checked the Microsoft Learn study guide, it showed the exam as retired on 30 June 2026, with the last skills outline grouped into envisioning and requirements, architecting the solution, and implementing and validating. I would tell anyone to re-check the official certification page for the current status and any successor, because these programmes change. The scenarios here teach the architecture thinking, which outlives any exam code.
questions.revision: The PL-600 study guide showed the exam retired on 30 June 2026. Re-check the official page for the current successor; the architecture skills remain valid.
questions.detailed:
## What was verified

When this material was prepared, the official Microsoft Learn **study guide for PL-600** (Microsoft Power Platform Solution Architect) carried a warning that the exam **retired on 30 June 2026**. The same guide described the last published skills outline (dated 23 September 2024) in three areas:

| Skill area | Weighting shown in that guide |
|---|---|
| Perform solution envisioning and requirement analysis | 45-50% |
| Architect a solution | 35-40% |
| Implement the solution | 15-20% |

Those figures are quoted from the guide as read, not estimated. Do not rely on them without opening the page yourself.

## What the areas contain

- **Envisioning and requirements:** solution planning, current-state processes, existing systems, functional and non-functional requirements, fit-gap analysis.
- **Architect a solution:** solution topology, environment strategy, data model, integrations, authentication, business continuity, security model, data loss prevention (DLP) policy choices.
- **Implement the solution:** validating designs, API limits, performance, go-live readiness.

## Status and successors

Third-party commentary suggests Microsoft points architects towards an agent-focused architect credential (often cited as AB-100), but sources disagree and some may be out of date. **Treat any successor name as unverified until you read the official Microsoft Learn certification page.** Also check renewal rules, prerequisites and whether existing credentials remain listed.

{{diagram:areas}}

## How to use the scenarios

Each scenario in this set gives a business case, options A to D, the best answer, why the others are weaker and the principle tested. The reasoning style (trade-offs, constraints, stakeholders) is what matters, whatever the exam is called today.

## Common mistakes

- Quoting weightings from memory or from blogs instead of the official page.
- Assuming a retired exam means the skills are obsolete. Fit-gap, security and environment design are still daily work.
- Treating passing an exam as proof of delivery experience.
followUps: How would you verify the current status of a Microsoft certification?
Which skill area would you prioritise for an enterprise agent role, and why?
How do you keep architecture knowledge current when exams are retired?

diagrams.title: PL-600 skill areas
diagrams.alt: Three connected skill areas of the Power Platform Solution Architect outline: envisioning and requirements leads to architecting the solution, which leads to implementing and validating it.

questions.title: Scenario: stakeholders list 80 requirements. How do you run discovery and fit-gap?
questions.quick: I would not start with the 80 items as a flat list. I group them into capabilities, separate functional from non-functional, and tie each to a business outcome and owner. Then I classify each as standard feature, configuration, extension or custom build, and note the risk and effort. Gaps go back to stakeholders with options, including process change. The result is a prioritised, agreed scope rather than an unbounded backlog.
questions.revision: Group requirements by capability and outcome, classify each as fit, configure, extend or build, and negotiate gaps with options including process change.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

A department sends **80 requirements** for a case-management solution on Power Platform. Many overlap, a few conflict, and none have owners. The sponsor wants a delivery date next week. How do you run discovery and fit-gap?

## Options

- **A.** Estimate each requirement as written and send the total.
- **B.** Group by capability, tie to outcomes, classify fit-gap, then agree scope with options for gaps.
- **C.** Start building the most visible screens and discover the rest in sprints.
- **D.** Reject requirements that look hard to build.

## Correct answer: B

Grouping exposes duplicates and conflicts, outcomes allow prioritisation, and classification (standard, configure, extend, custom, out of scope) shows where cost and risk sit.

| Classification | Meaning | Typical follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| Fit | Standard capability does it | Configure and demo |
| Configure | Needs setup, not code | Estimate small |
| Extend | Plug-in, custom connector, component | Estimate with risk |
| Gap | Not achievable cheaply | Options: change process, buy, or build |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** treats unclear requirements as precise, so the estimate is false precision.
- **C** builds before agreeing scope, which hides gaps until late.
- **D** replaces judgement with convenience and damages trust.

## Principle tested

**Requirements are hypotheses about outcomes.** Fit-gap converts them into decisions with owners, evidence and cost, and treats process change as a legitimate solution for a gap.

## Practical steps

1. Run workshops by process, not by department.
2. Record non-functional needs (volumes, availability, audit, residency) separately.
3. Prototype the riskiest few items early.
4. Keep a decision log of accepted gaps and who accepted them.

## Common mistakes

- Skipping non-functional requirements until testing.
- Accepting a gap silently instead of recording the trade-off.
- Letting the loudest stakeholder set priority.
followUps: How do you handle two stakeholders with conflicting requirements?
When is it right to recommend a purchased solution over a build?
What goes into a decision log for accepted gaps?

questions.title: Scenario: canvas app, model-driven app or portal for three user groups?
questions.quick: I choose by user and data shape, not by preference. Field staff needing a tailored mobile task flow suit a canvas app. Back-office caseworkers working across related Dataverse tables suit a model-driven app, which gives navigation, views, forms and security-aware behaviour quickly. External customers who are not licensed internal users suit a portal built with Power Pages. They can share one Dataverse model while each experience stays simple.
questions.revision: Canvas for tailored task flows, model-driven for data-rich internal work on Dataverse, Power Pages for external users. All three can share one data model.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

A utilities company has three groups: **field engineers** who capture inspections on tablets, often offline; **back-office caseworkers** who manage complex cases with many related records; and **customers** who need to submit and track requests.

## Options

- **A.** One canvas app for everyone.
- **B.** Canvas app for field engineers, model-driven app for caseworkers, Power Pages site for customers, sharing one Dataverse model.
- **C.** Model-driven app for everyone, giving customers licences.
- **D.** A custom web app for all three, ignoring low-code.

## Correct answer: B

| Group | Need | Best fit |
|---|---|---|
| Field engineers | Tailored, touch-first, possibly offline | Canvas app (check offline capability and limits for the design) |
| Caseworkers | Many related tables, views, process stages | Model-driven app |
| Customers | External identities, simple self-service | Power Pages |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** forces a data-heavy workflow into a layout you must build and maintain screen by screen.
- **C** is costly and awkward for external users, and licensing should be validated against current Microsoft guidance.
- **D** may be right in rare cases (extreme UX or scale needs) but discards productivity and governance without evidence of need.

## Principle tested

**Match the experience to the user and the data, and keep one source of truth.** Separate apps per persona, one data model, role-based security.

## Check before committing

- Licensing for each persona (verify on the official licensing guide).
- Offline needs and data volume.
- Accessibility and branding requirements.
- Who maintains each app.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing canvas because it looks flexible, then rebuilding model-driven behaviour by hand.
- Exposing internal tables directly to external users without a purpose-built permission layer.
- Ignoring licensing until late in the project.
followUps: What would push you towards a custom web app?
How do you design security when external users share a data model?
How do you decide whether offline is a real requirement?

questions.title: Scenario: store data in Dataverse, or connect to the external system with virtual tables?
questions.quick: I decide by who owns the data, how it is used and the limits. If Power Platform owns the process and needs relationships, security, auditing and offline, I store it in Dataverse. If another system remains the system of record and the data is read often but rarely changed here, a virtual table or connector avoids duplication. I check latency, delegation, throttling, feature support and failure behaviour, because virtual tables do not behave exactly like native tables.
questions.revision: Own it and need rich features: import to Dataverse. External system stays master and freshness matters: virtual table or connector, after checking limits.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

An ERP holds 12 million customer-order rows and remains the system of record. A new service app needs to show order history next to cases, and caseworkers add notes and tasks. The ERP exposes an OData API with moderate performance.

## Options

- **A.** Copy all ERP orders into Dataverse nightly.
- **B.** Keep cases, notes and tasks in Dataverse; surface orders through a virtual table (or API-backed connector) with a small cached summary where needed.
- **C.** Build every screen on direct connector calls with no Dataverse.
- **D.** Migrate the ERP orders permanently and retire the ERP.

## Correct answer: B

Cases and notes are owned by the new process, so they belong in Dataverse with security and audit. Orders belong to the ERP, so reading them live avoids stale duplicates and storage cost.

| Factor | Import | Virtual or live |
|---|---|---|
| Data freshness | As fresh as the sync | Live |
| Relationships, rollups, offline | Full | Limited (verify per feature) |
| Performance | Local | Depends on source |
| Source outage | App still works | Data unavailable |
| Storage cost | Higher | Lower |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** duplicates 12 million rows, introduces sync lag and conflict questions.
- **C** loses relationships, row-level security and a consistent model.
- **D** is a different programme with its own business case.

## Principle tested

**Single system of record, minimal duplication, and explicit trade-offs for each choice.** Test the virtual table with realistic volumes before committing.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming virtual tables support every Dataverse feature.
- Not designing the user experience for source outages.
- Syncing everything "just in case", paying storage and reconciliation costs.
followUps: What would make you import a subset rather than virtualise?
How do you handle source outages in the UI?
How would you test performance before deciding?

questions.title: Scenario: design the security model for regional teams, managers and contractors
questions.quick: I start from who needs to see and change what, then use the least complex mechanism that works. Business units and security roles control access by region, Microsoft Entra ID groups manage membership, and team ownership handles shared cases. Sensitive columns get column-level security, and contractors get a narrower role plus time-limited access. I avoid per-record sharing at scale, because it is hard to audit and slows performance.
questions.revision: Use business units and roles for regional scope, Entra groups for membership, column security for sensitive fields, and avoid heavy record-by-record sharing.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

A company has three regions. Regional staff must see only their region's cases, managers see all cases in their region, a central audit team sees everything read-only, and contractors need limited access for six months. Some columns (customer identifiers) are sensitive.

## Options

- **A.** One business unit; share each record manually with the right users.
- **B.** Business unit per region, role-based access, Entra ID groups, column-level security for sensitive fields, a read-only audit role and a time-bound contractor role.
- **C.** Give everyone a broad role and rely on app-level filters.
- **D.** Separate environment per region.

## Correct answer: B

| Requirement | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Regional separation | Business units and role access levels |
| Manager visibility | Role with business-unit depth |
| Cross-region audit | Separate read-only role |
| Sensitive fields | Column-level security profiles |
| Contractors | Narrow role, group-based, expiry reviewed |
| Membership | Entra ID groups mapped to teams |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** creates thousands of shares, which are hard to audit and can degrade performance.
- **C** is not security, because filters in an app do not stop access through other apps, APIs or exports.
- **D** is heavy and only justified by residency or isolation requirements, not simple row visibility.

## Principle tested

**Enforce security in the data layer, use the simplest model, and manage access through groups and reviews.**

## Design notes

- Document the role matrix and test with real personas.
- Plan joiner, mover and leaver processes.
- Consider DLP and external access separately.

## Common mistakes

- Cloning system roles and editing them without documentation.
- Using sharing as the main model.
- Forgetting that integrations run with their own identities and need least privilege too.
followUps: When would business units be the wrong tool?
How do you test a security model before go-live?
How do you handle a manager who moves region?

questions.title: Scenario: design the environment strategy and DLP policies for a growing tenant
questions.quick: I separate by purpose and risk. Development, test and production environments for each major solution, with a managed or controlled personal-productivity area for citizen makers. Tenant-level data loss prevention policies classify connectors into business, non-business and blocked groups, with environment-level exceptions only where justified. Ownership, naming, region and lifecycle are documented, and monitoring is in place before makers are invited in.
questions.revision: Separate dev, test and production per solution, a governed space for makers, tenant DLP baseline with justified exceptions, and clear ownership.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

A tenant has one default environment where 400 makers build apps. Finance wants a regulated solution, and the security team found a flow sending data to a personal storage connector.

## Options

- **A.** Keep everything in the default environment and train makers.
- **B.** Create dev, test and production environments for managed solutions; a governed environment for low-risk maker work; a tenant DLP baseline with documented exceptions.
- **C.** Block all connectors tenant-wide.
- **D.** One environment per maker.

## Correct answer: B

{{diagram:env}}

| Layer | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Default environment | Personal productivity, tightly limited |
| Maker or sandbox environments | Learning, with DLP and expiry |
| Dev, test, production | Managed solutions with ALM |
| Regulated environment | Stricter DLP, region, audit, restricted admins |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** mixes experiments with production and makes DLP exceptions impossible to scope.
- **C** stops legitimate work and drives shadow IT.
- **D** creates sprawl with no ownership.

## Principle tested

**Govern by risk tier, automate guardrails, and give makers a safe route.** Verify current Power Platform admin capabilities (managed environments, environment groups, DLP options) on official documentation.

## Common mistakes

- Setting DLP policies without a connector review.
- No environment lifecycle, so abandoned environments accumulate.
- Ignoring the region of the environment against data residency needs.
followUps: How would you handle a team that needs an exception to DLP?
What is the role of the Centre of Excellence toolkit here?
How do you stop environment sprawl?

diagrams.title: Environment tiers
diagrams.alt: Environment tiers: default environment for personal use, maker sandboxes, a dev to test to production chain for managed solutions, and a regulated environment, all under a tenant data loss prevention baseline.

questions.title: Scenario: cloud flow, custom connector or Azure integration for a critical order feed?
questions.quick: I choose by volume, reliability and ownership. A cloud flow suits low-to-moderate volume, business-owned automation with simple mapping. A custom connector standardises access to an API so many makers reuse it safely. For high volume, ordering, retries, transformation or strict reliability, I put Azure integration, such as Service Bus with Functions or Logic Apps, behind a well-defined API and let Power Platform call that.
questions.revision: Flows for modest business automation, custom connectors for reusable API access, Azure integration for high volume, strict reliability or complex transformation.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

Orders from a warehouse system must reach Dataverse. Volume is 200 per hour normally, 20,000 per hour at peak sales. Orders must not be lost or duplicated, and the warehouse API sometimes fails.

## Options

- **A.** A scheduled cloud flow polling the warehouse API.
- **B.** A custom connector to the warehouse API, called from many flows.
- **C.** Warehouse publishes to Azure Service Bus; a Function or Logic App consumes with retries, idempotency and dead-lettering, writing to Dataverse.
- **D.** Users re-key orders manually.

## Correct answer: C

{{diagram:int}}

| Option | Strength | Weakness here |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud flow | Quick, business-owned | Throughput and plan limits, limited retry control |
| Custom connector | Reusable, governed access | Does not solve buffering or reliability |
| Service Bus plus Azure compute | Buffering, retry, dead-letter, scale | More engineering and cost |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** may miss peaks and duplicates on retry.
- **B** is useful but is an access layer, not a reliability pattern. It could be combined with C.
- **D** is a failure of design.

## Principle tested

**Decouple producers and consumers when load and reliability demand it, and keep low-code for where it is strong.** Check current Dataverse service protection limits and connector throttling before sizing.

## Common mistakes

- Using flows for bulk integration then fighting throttling.
- Not making the consumer idempotent.
- No dead-letter ownership: messages pile up silently.
followUps: How would you make the Dataverse write idempotent?
When would a custom connector still be worth adding?
What would you monitor on this integration?

diagrams.title: Order feed integration
diagrams.alt: Warehouse system publishes orders to Service Bus. A consumer function reads with retries, writes to Dataverse idempotently, and sends failures to a dead-letter queue that is monitored.

questions.title: Scenario: design the ALM and solution strategy for three teams building one product
questions.quick: I put everything in solutions, use a single publisher, and separate by layers: a core solution and dependent feature solutions, to avoid circular dependencies. Source control holds unpacked solutions, a pipeline builds managed solutions and promotes them from development to test to production with approvals. Environment variables and connection references handle environment differences. Hotfixes follow a defined branch route, and nobody edits production directly.
questions.revision: Everything in solutions, one publisher, layered core and feature solutions, source control, automated managed deployments, environment variables and no production edits.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

Three teams build one product. Releases are manual exports; last month someone fixed a flow directly in production and the next deployment overwrote it.

## Options

- **A.** Keep manual exports but add a checklist.
- **B.** Layered solutions, source control, automated pipelines deploying managed solutions with environment variables and connection references, and a no-edit-in-production rule.
- **C.** One giant solution for all teams.
- **D.** Each team deploys independently with its own publisher.

## Correct answer: B

| Element | Why |
|---|---|
| Layered solutions | Controls dependencies and team ownership |
| Source control | History, review, rollback |
| Pipeline (Power Platform Pipelines, Azure DevOps or GitHub, verify current tooling) | Repeatable, auditable |
| Managed solutions in test and production | Clean upgrade and removal |
| Environment variables and connection references | Config without rebuild |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** relies on memory, which already failed.
- **C** creates merge conflicts and long release trains.
- **D** causes publisher sprawl and dependency conflicts.

## Principle tested

**Treat low-code assets as software: version, review, test, deploy through a pipeline.** Include automated checks (solution checker, tests) in the pipeline.

## Common mistakes

- Unmanaged solutions in production.
- Hard-coded URLs and connection details.
- No plan for hotfixes, so people edit production under pressure.
- Not testing upgrades, only fresh installs.
followUps: How do you handle a hotfix?
How do you avoid circular dependencies between solutions?
What gates would you place before production?

questions.title: Scenario: the app is slow and flows are throttled after go-live. How do you diagnose it?
questions.quick: I measure before I change anything. For the app, I check form load, number of controls and data calls, delegation warnings and query design. For flows and integrations, I check request volume against service protection and connector limits, concurrency, loops and retries. Then I fix the largest cause first, such as reducing calls, batching, filtering server-side, or moving heavy work to asynchronous processing, and I add monitoring so we see limits before users do.
questions.revision: Measure first. Reduce calls, filter server-side, batch, control concurrency, move heavy work to async, and monitor limits before users notice.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

Two weeks after go-live, a canvas app takes 12 seconds to open and a flow that processes records fails intermittently with throttling responses.

## Options

- **A.** Buy more licences and hope limits rise.
- **B.** Profile the app and flows, fix the largest causes (calls, delegation, loops, concurrency), batch or move heavy work to asynchronous processing, and add monitoring.
- **C.** Rewrite everything as a custom app.
- **D.** Ask users to avoid peak hours.

## Correct answer: B

| Symptom | Likely cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Slow app open | Many data calls on start, large collections | Load on demand, reduce controls, cache |
| Wrong or partial results | Non-delegable queries | Redesign filters, use delegable operations |
| Throttled flows | Bursts, high concurrency | Throttle concurrency, batch, retry with back-off |
| Timeouts | Long synchronous work | Queue and process asynchronously |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** treats limits as purchasable without evidence. Some capacity can be added, but the design cost remains.
- **C** is disproportionate before profiling.
- **D** pushes the problem to users.

## Principle tested

**Design for the documented limits and measure real behaviour.** Check current service protection limits, request allocations and delegation documentation, because they change.

## Common mistakes

- Testing with 50 rows then going live with 5 million.
- Looping row by row when a batch call exists.
- No telemetry, so diagnosis begins only after complaints.
followUps: How do you load-test a Power Platform solution?
What is delegation and how do you spot a problem?
How would you design retries without worsening throttling?

questions.title: Scenario: migrate 8 million legacy records into Dataverse. What approach do you take?
questions.quick: I treat migration as its own workstream. First profile and clean the source, agree mapping and ownership, and decide what not to migrate. Load reference data first, then dependent records, using a tool suited to volume, with trial loads, reconciliation counts and sample checks. I plan a cutover with a freeze window or delta load, a rollback decision point and business sign-off on results, not just on completed jobs.
questions.revision: Profile and clean, agree mapping, load in dependency order with trial runs, reconcile counts and samples, then cutover with a rollback point and sign-off.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

A legacy system holds 8 million records of mixed quality. The business wants a weekend cutover, with all history, and no downtime for customers on Monday.

## Options

- **A.** Export everything and import in one run on Saturday.
- **B.** Profile, clean and map; migrate only agreed scope; run several trial loads with reconciliation; do a final delta load in a freeze window with rollback criteria.
- **C.** Migrate nothing and ask users to re-enter data.
- **D.** Migrate everything, then fix quality issues in production.

## Correct answer: B

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| Scope | Decide active versus archive data; archive may stay elsewhere |
| Mapping | Source to target, with transformations and owners |
| Order | Reference data, parents, then children and relationships |
| Trial loads | Measure duration, errors, throttling |
| Reconciliation | Counts, totals, sampled record comparison |
| Cutover | Freeze, delta, validate, go or roll back |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** has no rehearsal, so duration and defects are unknown.
- **C** may be right for tiny datasets but not for this one.
- **D** brings dirty data into live processes and erodes trust.

## Principle tested

**Rehearse, reconcile and keep a rollback decision.** Consider storage costs and the option of archiving history outside Dataverse.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting ownership, security and audit fields in the mapping.
- Not testing relationships and lookups.
- Declaring success when jobs finish rather than when the business validates data.
followUps: How do you decide what history to leave behind?
How do you handle records changed during cutover?
Which tools would you consider for the load?

questions.title: Scenario: leadership wants Copilot and agents everywhere. How do you govern adoption?
questions.quick: I start with use cases that have clear value and bounded risk, rather than switching everything on. I review data sources and permissions, because an agent can only be as safe as the data it can reach. I set guardrails: approved connectors and knowledge sources, authentication, content moderation, human approval for consequential actions, logging and evaluation. Then I pilot, measure, and expand with an owner and review process for every agent.
questions.revision: Pick bounded use cases, fix data permissions first, set guardrails and approvals for actions, log and evaluate, then pilot before scaling.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

The executive team wants agents for HR, finance and customer service within a quarter. Document libraries have inconsistent permissions, and one proposed agent could issue refunds.

## Options

- **A.** Enable everything and let makers experiment.
- **B.** Pilot bounded use cases, remediate data permissions, define guardrails and human approval for consequential actions, log and evaluate, then scale with named owners.
- **C.** Ban agents until all risks are removed.
- **D.** Let each department choose its own platform with no central view.

## Correct answer: B

| Control | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Knowledge-source review | Prevent exposing over-shared content |
| Authentication and user identity pass-through | Respect user permissions |
| Approved connectors and actions | Limit blast radius |
| Human approval for refunds and similar actions | Contain consequences |
| Logging, evaluation sets | Detect wrong answers and misuse |
| Owner and lifecycle | Avoid orphaned agents |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** surfaces oversharing at scale, and nobody owns incidents.
- **C** is unrealistic and pushes use to unmanaged tools.
- **D** fragments governance and cost visibility.

## Principle tested

**Governance enables adoption.** Match autonomy to risk, and verify product capabilities and licensing against current Microsoft documentation, since agent features change quickly.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the model as the only risk and ignoring data permissions.
- No evaluation set, so quality is judged by anecdotes.
- No exit plan for an agent that misbehaves.
followUps: Which actions should always need human approval?
How would you evaluate an agent before launch?
How do you handle makers who build agents outside the process?

questions.title: Scenario: the solution is live but users still use spreadsheets. What went wrong?
questions.quick: Low adoption is usually a change problem, not a technology one. I would ask users why: is the app slower, missing something they need, or has nobody removed the old way? Then I fix friction fast, involve champions in each team, give role-based training in context, make leaders use the new reports, and set a retirement date for the spreadsheet. I track adoption and outcome measures, not just logins.
questions.revision: Diagnose why users avoid it, fix friction, use champions and role-based training, retire the old process, and measure outcomes as well as usage.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

A case-tracking app went live six weeks ago. Managers still ask for weekly spreadsheets, and staff keep personal copies "just in case".

## Options

- **A.** Send a reminder email and wait.
- **B.** Interview users, fix friction, add champions and targeted training, stop accepting spreadsheet reporting and set a retirement date.
- **C.** Add more features immediately.
- **D.** Lock the spreadsheets and give no warning.

## Correct answer: B

| Cause | Response |
|---|---|
| Missing data or slow steps | Prioritise quick fixes, show visible progress |
| Unclear benefit | Share outcome measures in team meetings |
| No leadership pull | Managers use app reports only |
| Training too generic | Role-based, task-based, short |
| Old process still allowed | Agreed retirement date and support |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** assumes the cause is forgetfulness.
- **C** adds complexity before understanding the barrier.
- **D** damages trust and may break real work.

## Principle tested

**Adoption is designed.** Include change management, communications, support and measurement in the solution plan from the start, with sponsor commitment.

## Metrics worth tracking

- Active use by role, not total logins.
- Time to complete key tasks versus baseline.
- Data quality and completeness.
- Number of requests for the old reports.

## Common mistakes

- Treating training as a single go-live session.
- No feedback loop after launch.
- Measuring success by delivery date.
followUps: How would you pick champions?
What would you do if the sponsor stops pushing the change?
How do you separate a usability problem from a resistance problem?

questions.title: How do you build a non-functional requirements matrix for a Power Platform solution?
questions.quick: I turn vague words like fast, secure and reliable into measurable targets with owners. For each category I record the requirement, the metric, the target, how it will be tested and which design decision satisfies it. Categories include performance, availability, recovery, security, compliance, scalability, accessibility, supportability and cost. I tie them to the Power Platform Well-Architected pillars as a checklist and revisit them at design review and before go-live.
questions.revision: Turn vague qualities into measurable targets with owner, test method and design response, across performance, availability, security, compliance, cost and support.
questions.detailed:
## Purpose

Non-functional requirements (NFRs) decide whether a solution that works in a demo also works on a busy Monday. A matrix makes them visible, testable and negotiable.

## Matrix template

| Category | Example requirement | Metric and target (placeholder) | How tested | Design response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Performance | Case form opens quickly | P95 under [X] seconds | Load and UI timing test | Lean forms, indexed queries |
| Availability | Service available in business hours | [Y]% monthly | Monitoring, incident review | Dependencies reviewed |
| Recovery | Restore after failure | RTO [a] hours, RPO [b] hours | DR rehearsal | Backups, runbook |
| Security | Least privilege | No broad roles | Role review, pen test | Security model |
| Compliance | Data stays in region | Region list | Environment audit | Regional environment |
| Scalability | Peak volume | [N] records per hour | Peak test | Async patterns |
| Accessibility | Standards compliance | Agreed standard | Audit | Component choices |
| Supportability | Diagnose within an hour | Telemetry in place | Support drill | Logging, alerts |
| Cost | Run cost ceiling | Budget per month | Cost review | Right-sized capacity |

Targets above are placeholders to agree with the business, not recommendations.

## Process

1. Workshop with business, security, operations and support.
2. Rank by risk, then agree targets and owners.
3. Link each to a design decision and a test.
4. Review the matrix at design review, UAT and go-live.

## Common mistakes

- Writing "the system must be fast" with no number.
- Leaving NFRs to the end, when changing the design is expensive.
- Setting targets the platform or budget cannot meet, without saying so.
- Forgetting that integrations and licences have limits too.
followUps: Which NFRs most often conflict with each other?
How do you test recovery targets?
How do the Well-Architected pillars help here?

questions.title: Scenario: how do you document the architecture and keep stakeholders aligned?
questions.quick: I keep documentation light but decisive. A context diagram for everyone, a solution topology and data flow for engineers, a security and environment view for risk teams, and a decision log recording options, trade-offs and who agreed. I tailor the message to each audience, hold regular design reviews, and keep the documents in one versioned place so they change with the solution rather than rotting after sign-off.
questions.revision: Context diagram, topology, security view and a decision log, tailored per audience, versioned in one place and reviewed regularly.
questions.detailed:
## Scenario

Three vendors and two internal teams are building parts of a platform. Meetings produce conflicting assumptions, the security team has not seen the data flows, and a sponsor asks, "what are we actually building?"

## Options

- **A.** One 120-page design document signed off once.
- **B.** A small set of audience-specific views plus a decision log, versioned and reviewed regularly.
- **C.** Verbal agreement in meetings.
- **D.** Let each vendor document its own part.

## Correct answer: B

| Artefact | Audience | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Context diagram | Sponsors, all | Systems, users, boundaries |
| Solution topology | Engineers | Components, environments, integrations |
| Data flow and security view | Security, compliance | Data movement, identities, residency |
| Decision log | Everyone | Decision, options, trade-offs, owner, date |
| NFR matrix | Delivery, operations | Targets and tests |

## Why the others are weaker

- **A** is rarely read and quickly outdated.
- **C** leaves no record and invites later dispute.
- **D** produces parts, not a coherent whole.

## Principle tested

**Communication is part of architecture.** Decisions that are written, owned and visible are decisions that survive staff changes.

## Habits

- Review the diagrams with the people who must build and operate them.
- Record rejected options as well as the chosen one.
- Keep a short list of open risks with owners.

## Common mistakes

- Diagrams that mix business and technical levels.
- Sign-off treated as the end of communication.
- Hiding unresolved disagreements in vague wording.
followUps: What goes into a good decision record?
How do you handle a stakeholder who disagrees with a decision?
How often should the architecture be reviewed?

questions.title: If asked whether you hold the PL-600 certification, how do you answer honestly and close the gap?
questions.quick: I answer plainly: either I hold it or I do not, and I never imply otherwise. If I do not, I say what I do have, such as delivery experience and related learning, and that I know the exam has been retired or changed, so I would target whichever current credential Microsoft lists. I then describe a concrete plan: map the skills outline to my experience, fill gaps with labs, and schedule a date.
questions.revision: State your status plainly, show real experience, acknowledge the exam may have changed, and give a dated plan to close the gap.
questions.detailed:
## The honest answer

Interviewers value clarity over polish. A good answer has four parts:

1. **State the fact.** Hold it, do not hold it, or held it and it has lapsed. No hedging.
2. **Offer evidence you can defend.** Describe real solutions, decisions and outcomes, and the trade-offs you made.
3. **Show you know the landscape.** PL-600 was shown as retired on 30 June 2026 in the study guide when checked. Say you would verify the current Microsoft credential before booking anything.
4. **Present the plan.** Dated, specific and realistic.

## Example wording (generic)

"I do not currently hold it. I have led [type of delivery] and made decisions on [areas]. I know that exam has been retired, so I would confirm the current architect credential on Microsoft Learn and aim to sit it within [N] months."

## A practical gap-closing plan

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Download the current official skills outline and rate yourself on each line |
| 2 | List real experience that evidences each strong area |
| 3 | For weak areas, build a small lab or review documentation |
| 4 | Practise scenario questions and explain answers aloud |
| 5 | Use the official practice assessment if available |
| 6 | Book the exam date to create commitment |

## Remember

Exam preparation is not production experience. A certificate shows structured knowledge. Delivery experience shows judgement under constraints. Be clear about which is which.

## Common mistakes

- Implying a certification you do not have.
- Blaming the retirement as an excuse rather than showing a plan.
- Memorising answers without understanding trade-offs.
- Quoting skill weightings from memory.
followUps: How do you evidence architecture experience without naming a client?
What would you study first and why?
How would you answer if the interviewer pressed on a skill you have not used in production?
